summary: Explains how the Network Information Center at SRI handled documents for the ARPANET community. It says all information the center holds is open to any network participant, and it suggests ways sites can help the flow of documents. It is administrative guidance from 1971 rather than a technical protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 115 explains how the Network Information Center recorded and indexed network documents. It asks authors to provide useful details and describes how revised pages or new editions should be identified.

subtitle: NIC policies for cataloging, identifying, and revising network documents.

tldr.problem: Network participants needed shared ways to identify, find, catalog, and revise the growing collection of reports and memos.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC assigns unique NIC numbers, records standard descriptive fields in catalogs, creates indexes and subcollections, and sets page-based revision procedures.
tldr.outcome: RFC 115 describes NIC document-handling practices and asks document originators to supply consistent catalog information.

today: RFC 115 describes the NIC's document-handling practices in 1971. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: NIC Numbers and Open Information
sections.content:
The Network Information Center (NIC) says its purpose is to help information flow between network sites. It states that information it handles is available to any Network participant and that information sent to the NIC for recording or distribution is presumed unclassified and without distribution limits.

The NIC assigns each item a serial NIC number. The number has no intrinsic meaning and does not necessarily show issue order; it is a unique identifier for communication, indexing, and numeric filing.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC gives each document a unique number so people can refer to and find it. The number is an identifier, not a ranking or date.

sections.title: Catalogs, Listings, and Indexes
sections.content:
NIC staff record standard data about each item, including author, title, date, keywords, and an abstract, in coded statements. The Master Catalog contains these statements; the NIC Catalog is a subset marked for NIC.

Programs use the statements to produce listings by author and NIC number and indexes by author and keyword. The listings can indicate which Stations hold an item, while the indexes point to the larger catalog. Groups of documents can also be cataloged as retrievable subcollections.
sections.plainLanguage: The catalog stores a description of each document and can sort records in different ways. Groups of related documents can be collected so participants can retrieve them together.

sections.title: Information Authors Should Supply
sections.content:
For memos, originators should provide authors and addresses, addressees and addresses, the date, and the subject. For reports and formal documents, the essential fields include authors and addresses, title, date, abstract, and keywords.

The RFC says a short abstract of 150 to 200 words is important. It recommends author-supplied keywords, preferably from a standard thesaurus, and asks authors to identify when a document supersedes an earlier one.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors should include names, dates, titles, and other details that help the NIC catalog a document. Reports should also have a short abstract and keywords.

sections.title: Revising Functional Documents
sections.content:
A functional document keeps its title and purpose while its contents change. The RFC recommends looseleaf format for documents expected to be revised.

A substantial revision gets a new document and NIC number. Smaller changes use revised or inserted pages marked with the original document number and a revision date. Revisions should replace, add, or delete full pages; the NIC says it will not revise its own publications with errata lists.
sections.plainLanguage: A major revision gets a new document number. Smaller revisions replace or add whole pages with dates so readers can identify their version.
